conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived. We’ll be using a short, well-studied questionnaire called the EPDS (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). It’s simply ten questions about the past seven days, and it helps us spot any signs of postpartum depression or anxiety so we can offer the right support. Everything you share stays between you, me, and the clinical team unless safety is a concern, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you. Ready to begin?

Over the last week, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?
Honestly… not very often. I’ll smile once in a while if something cute happens with the baby, but I don’t really laugh the way I used to. It feels like the joy just isn’t there most of the time.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Most days I haven’t. I might manage a little smile if the baby does something cute, but I haven’t really laughed at anything in the past week.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just watching a show I liked—but this week nothing feels worth the effort. I’ll think “I should want to do that,” but then I feel too tired or just… flat, like it won’t actually feel good anyway.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby’s fussy or won’t settle, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—like I’m not feeding him right or I’m missing some cue. Yesterday he cried for almost an hour and I kept replaying it, telling myself a “good mom” would’ve calmed him faster. I know rationally babies just cry, but I still feel it’s my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting there with the baby sleeping soundly, but I’m still scanning the monitor, listening for every tiny noise, sure something’s wrong. My heart races, and I can’t settle even when nothing’s happening. I know it’s “for no good reason,” but I can’t switch it off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes, a few times this week. It hits suddenly—like last night while I was folding laundry, my chest tightened and I felt I couldn’t breathe properly. There was nothing going on, but for a minute I was sure something awful was about to happen. It passed after a bit, but the feeling keeps popping up out of nowhere.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, yeah. It’s like the second I open my eyes the list starts—feed him, change him, try to eat something, maybe shower, maybe answer one text—and it feels impossible. I’ll sit on the couch with the baby in my arms and just stare at the mess around me thinking, “I can’t keep up, I’m drowning,” even though it’s just normal newborn stuff.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

That’s been happening several nights this week. I’ll finally get the baby down, but then I’m lying there with my mind racing—worrying I forgot something, replaying every little cry, telling myself I’m failing. Even when I’m exhausted, it takes me forever to fall asleep, and when I do I jolt awake at every tiny sound.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah, pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding the baby or just sitting there and this heavy sadness rolls in. Sometimes I tear up without even knowing why. It’s like a gray cloud that won’t lift, even when nothing bad has happened.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

A few times this week. Nothing huge sets it off—yesterday it was just seeing a picture of myself pregnant on my phone. I started crying and couldn’t stop for ten minutes. It’s like the tears are sitting right under the surface all the time.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I haven’t had any thoughts like that. I feel overwhelmed and low, but I haven’t wanted to hurt myself.

You've shared that the past week has felt heavy and overwhelming-laughter and excitement seem distant, while sadness, self-blame, and constant worry fill your days. Despite loving your baby, you feel buried under a "gray cloud," crying easily, unable to sleep even when the house is quiet, and panicking without warning.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient explicitly states she has not laughed at all and only manages occasional faint smiles, aligning with "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient conveys near-complete loss of anticipatory pleasure, describing activities that once brought joy as now feeling pointless or too exhausting, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, intense self-blame for normal infant behavior, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports daily, uncontrollable, physiologically-intensified worry despite the baby being safe, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple sudden panic episodes this week without clear triggers, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily overwhelm, inability to manage routine newborn tasks, and feeling of drowning, aligning with "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple nights per week of significant sleep difficulty due to racing thoughts and worry about motherhood, matching 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>The patient describes experiencing sadness "pretty much every day," frequent tearfulness, and a persistent "gray cloud"—semantically matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Response indicates frequent crying triggered by minor stimuli, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 25 places you well above the cutoff for probable <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>, meeting core criteria: depressed mood most of the day, diminished interest/pleasure, self-reproach, fatigue, sleep disturbance, and impaired concentration/decision-making. High anxiety items also suggest comorbid <med>postpartum anxiety</med>. <quote>I can't keep up, I'm drowning</quote> signals functional impairment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> to discuss results and treatment options
2. Request referral to a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> or psychiatrist familiar with postpartum mood disorders
3. Reach out today to <med>Postpartum Support International</med> (1-800-944-4773) for 24/7 support and local resources
4. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med> or sertraline, both compatible with breastfeeding
5. Enlist practical help-partner, family, or postpartum doula for night feeds and household tasks so you can rest
6. Practice brief self-compassion breaks: set a 5-minute timer to breathe slowly and remind yourself <quote>this is the illness, not my fault</quote>
7. Plan daily 10-minute outdoor walks; sunlight and gentle movement can modestly lift mood and improve sleep
8. Keep the next pediatric visit-mention your mood so your providers can coordinate care for you and baby
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: Postpartum mother, 1 week post-delivery (approx.)

Presenting Symptoms / Behavioral Observations  
- Persistent low mood, sadness “pretty much every day”  
- Marked anhedonia: reports no enjoyment in previously pleasurable activities  
- Daily tearfulness; crying episodes triggered by minor cues  
- Excessive self-blame/guilt regarding infant care (“good mom would have…”)  
- Difficulty sleeping: initial insomnia even when infant is settled  
- Overwhelming fatigue, sense of “drowning,” difficulty completing basic tasks  
- Free-floating anxiety: near-constant worry, scanning for danger, heart racing  
- Sudden panic-like episodes (chest tightness, breathlessness) without precipitant  
- No reported self-harm ideation (endorsed item 10 negatively)

Pattern / Consistency  
Symptoms cluster into two domains:  
(1) Depressive: low mood, anhedonia, guilt, tearfulness, sleep/mood link  
(2) Anxiety: pervasive worry, panic symptoms, hypervigilance regarding infant

Screening Significance  
Responses are consistent with elevated risk for postpartum depression and comorbid postpartum anxiety. Items reflecting mood, enjoyment, coping, and sleep are endorsed at high frequency/intensity.

Risk Factors Identified  
- Persistent depressive symptoms > 2 weeks  
- Functional impairment (self-care, household tasks)  
- Sleep disruption secondary to mood rather than infant needs alone  
- Excessive maternal guilt/self-criticism  
- Presence of spontaneous panic symptoms  
- Absence of self-harm/suicidal ideation (current protective factor)

Overall Screening Impression  
Patient scores in high-risk range for postpartum depressive and anxiety symptoms, with notable impairment in daily functioning. Further clinical assessment recommended to determine diagnostic status and intervention needs; safety plan reviewed—no acute self-harm concerns at present.
